name: Mount Seymour Backcountry
access: BC Parks backcountry kiosk at the north end of lot P4, Mount Seymour Provincial Park, North Vancouver. Park in P1 or Lower P5 without a resort pass; a free BC Parks day-use pass is needed there on winter peak days. BC Parks marks two uptracks from the kiosk, mid-December to March 31; no dogs in the backcountry.
summary: The closest backcountry to Vancouver: a trail past the resort to Pump Peak, Tim Jones Peak and Mount Seymour's summit.
overview: Seymour is where many Vancouver skiers and snowshoers take their first steps beyond a ski area. The terrain is small but real, and fog and steep drop-offs on the far side of the peaks have led to many rescues of lost parties.
route_description: The route follows the marked trail beside the resort, then climbs over the bumps toward Seymour's summit. Most parties turn around and return the same way.
hazards: Fog and navigation errors, cliffs and gullies off the back side, and avalanche slopes on the summit approaches.
skills: Basic navigation, avalanche gear and awareness; AST 1 for anything beyond the trail.
go_guided: An easy half-day intro to winter travel close to the city.
author: Ross Berg

name: Howe Sound Crest Trail
access: Cypress Mountain to Porteau Cove (car shuttle)
summary: A rugged ridge traverse above Howe Sound from Cypress to Porteau Cove, past the Lions and Brunswick Mountain.
overview: The HSCT is Vancouver's big mountain run: a rough, exposed trail that rolls over peaks and passes with ocean views the whole way. It is much harder and slower than its distance suggests.
route_description: From Cypress the trail climbs past the Lions and continues north along the ridge over steep ups and downs, then drops to Porteau Cove on Highway 99.
hazards: Steep exposed sections, lingering snow early in the season, few water sources, and a long exit if things go wrong.
skills: Strong mountain-running fitness and scrambling comfort.
go_guided: A great objective for a custom guided running day.
author: Ross Berg
verify: Distance, gain, and whether we guide it.

name: Squamish Buttress
access: Stawamus Chief Provincial Park
summary: The classic way up the Chief's south end: Apron slabs, then six pitches on the buttress to 5.10c, finishing on the First Peak.
overview: Squamish Buttress is the route of our Challenge the Chief day. People who have only top-roped in a gym follow a guide all the way to the top, learning belay changeovers, multi-pitch anchors and rappels on the way. The views of Howe Sound and the Squamish valley from the buttress are among the best in town.
route_description: The day starts on the Apron slabs above the parking lot, and a climbers' trail through the trees leads to the base of the buttress. Pitches of slab, blocky corners and a steep finger-crack crux climb the buttress to the ledges below Raven's Castle, and easy ground leads to the First Peak. The descent is a hike back down the Chief trail.
hazards: Exposure, rockfall from parties above, summer heat on the south face and busy weekends.
skills: To follow with a guide: top-roped 5.6 in a gym. To lead: solid 5.10c trad and multi-pitch systems.
go_guided: Challenge the Chief: no outdoor experience needed, just gym top-roping at 5.6.
author: Ross Berg
verify: Grade (5.10c), pitches (6 on the buttress) and approach checked – see Verify log. Your call: which Apron route you use on Challenge the Chief. The description now says the day starts on the Apron (no source supports hiking the Chief trail to the base). ≈330 m only holds if the Apron counts; the buttress alone is ≈182 m.

name: Angel's Crest
access: Stawamus Chief Provincial Park
summary: Thirteen pitches up the forested north ridge of the Chief, past the Acrophobe Towers, to the second summit.
overview: Angel's Crest feels like an alpine route a few minutes from town. It weaves along the crest of the ridge with short walls, a famous crack pitch and the airy Acrophobe Towers, and finishes with a 5.8 squeeze chimney onto the summit of the Second Peak. It has been a staple of our guiding since the start.
route_description: A short approach on the North Gully trail leads to the start of the ridge. The route follows the crest through forested ledges and steep walls to the Acrophobe Towers and on to the Second Peak. The descent follows the Chief hiking trail.
hazards: Long day with route-finding between pitches, loose rock on ledges, rockfall in the North Gully and on its approach trail, and slower parties ahead.
skills: To follow with a guide: comfortable top-roping 5.8–5.9. To lead: 5.10 trad and efficient multi-pitch.
go_guided: A guided Angel's Crest is the perfect next step after Challenge the Chief.
author: Ross Berg
verify: Summit checked: tops out on the Second Peak (655 m); last pitch is a 5.8 squeeze chimney, not 5.7 (overview fixed). Your call: follower prerequisite – the row says top-roping 5.8–5.9, your Custom Multi-Pitch page only gives the general 5.6 minimum.

name: The Grand Wall
access: Stawamus Chief Provincial Park
summary: Squamish's most famous climb: the Split Pillar, the Sword and Bellygood Ledge up the centre of the Chief.
overview: The Grand Wall climbs straight up the middle of the Chief's main face and is on almost every climber's tick list. The Split Pillar is the crack people travel for. A short aid section makes it possible at 5.11a with a few moves on gear.
route_description: The route starts from the base of the main face, climbs the Split Pillar and the Sword, then traverses Bellygood Ledge to finish. Descent is by the Chief trail.
hazards: Sustained difficulty, exposure on Bellygood Ledge, crowds and heat.
skills: To follow: confident on 5.10 cracks. To lead: strong 5.11 trad.
go_guided: Following a guide lets you climb the Grand Wall without leading the hard pitches.
author: Ross Berg

name: Diedre
access: The Apron, Stawamus Chief Provincial Park
summary: The classic first multi-pitch in Squamish: a long right-facing corner up the Apron slabs.
overview: Diedre follows one clean corner up the Apron for six pitches of friction slab and hand cracks. It is the climb that turns gym climbers into rock climbers, and it is often busy for good reason.
route_description: A short walk from the parking lot and a scramble up a gully and ledges lead to the base on the Apron. The route follows the corner to the top of the slab, and most parties walk off along Broadway Ledge and down the Apron descent trail through the forest.
hazards: Polished slab when wet, run-out sections on the second and last pitches, queues at belays, and rockfall from parties above.
skills: To follow: top-roped 5.6–5.7. To lead: comfortable 5.8 trad on slab.
go_guided: A common first day on our multi-pitch course.
author: Ross Berg

name: Skywalker
access: Shannon Falls area
summary: A fun moderate multi-pitch near Shannon Falls, a good alternative when the Apron is busy.
overview: Skywalker gives a few pitches of varied 5.8 climbing with views over Howe Sound. It works well as a first or second multi-pitch day.
route_description: A short approach leads to the base. Several pitches climb to the top, followed by a descent back to the trail.
hazards: Wet rock after rain and route-finding on the descent.
skills: To follow: top-roped 5.7. To lead: 5.8 trad.
go_guided: Often climbed on our multi-pitch courses and custom days.
author: Ross Berg

name: Smoke Bluffs
access: Smoke Bluffs Park, downtown Squamish
summary: Hundreds of short granite cracks and slabs a few minutes' walk from downtown Squamish.
overview: The Smoke Bluffs are where Squamish climbers learn. Short approaches, lots of easy and moderate routes, and walls that dry fast make it the go-to for intro days, trad leading and crack technique. Classics like Pipeline are a rite of passage.
route_description: Trails from the park's parking lots lead to dozens of small walls. Most routes are one pitch with top-rope anchors or walk-off tops.
hazards: Busy walls, loose rock at tops of cliffs, and children and dogs at the base.
skills: None to start with a guide. Leading here means learning gear placements and anchors.
go_guided: Our intro, trad and crack courses run here.

name: Sky Pilot Mountain
time: 1 day (max 11 h when the gondola runs late) or 3 days
access: Sea to Sky Gondola, Squamish
summary: The closest real alpine summit to Squamish and Vancouver: glacier, snow and scrambling to a 2,031 m summit above Howe Sound.
overview: The Sea to Sky Gondola saves almost a vertical kilometre of approach, putting Sky Pilot and the Stadium Glacier within a day's reach. It feels like a big mountain: a glacier, steep snow, fourth-class rock and a summit with views from the Tantalus to the ocean.
route_description: From the top of the gondola, the approach follows an old logging road to the mountain. The route crosses the Stadium Glacier and gains the West Ridge, where fourth and easy fifth-class rock leads to the summit. The descent returns the same way to the gondola.
hazards: Glacier travel, steep snow in early summer, loose rock and gondola closing times on a long day.
skills: Some rock climbing (top-roped 5.6), fitness for 8+ hours of movement.
go_guided: One of our most popular first alpine summits, as a day or a 3-day trip with Co-Pilot.
author: Ross Berg

name: Mount Habrich
access: Sea to Sky Gondola, Squamish
summary: A granite fin above the Sea to Sky Gondola with alpine rock routes on its south and west faces.
overview: Habrich is Sky Pilot's steeper neighbour, a clean granite summit with real climbing to reach the top. Our trips have climbed the south face and rappelled the west face, with views straight across to Sky Pilot and Co-Pilot.
route_description: From the gondola an old logging road and climbers' trail lead to the base. Routes on the south face climb to the summit, and descent is by rappels down the west face.
hazards: Exposure, loose blocks, lingering snow in the gullies early in the season.
skills: Comfortable following 5.7–5.8 in mountain boots or approach shoes.
go_guided: Available as a custom day; pairs well with Sky Pilot on a multi-day trip.
author: Ross Berg

name: Mount Tricouni North Ridge
access: 4x4 road west of Highway 99, between Squamish and Whistler
summary: One of the quickest and best alpine rock routes in the Coast Mountains: an exposed 5.4 ridge to a summit above both valleys.
overview: A 4x4 road almost into the alpine and a short meadow approach make Tricouni a full alpine day without the long walk. The ridge itself is striking and exposed but never hard, and the summit looks over both the Squamish and Whistler valleys.
route_description: After a 1–2 hour walk through alpine meadows, the route crosses the small north glacier to reach the ridge. The ridge is followed to the summit, then descended.
hazards: Exposure on the ridge, a moat and snow on the glacier crossing, and road conditions on the 4x4 approach.
skills: Some alpine or rock experience; good fitness for 8–12 hours.
go_guided: A perfect one-day introduction to alpine rock ridges.

name: Stawamus Chief Trail (Three Peaks)
grade: Steep trail with chains and ladders
time: 2–4 hours running; 5–7 hours hiking all three peaks
access: Stawamus Chief Provincial Park, Squamish
summary: Squamish's signature hike: steep stairs and ladders to all three summits of the Chief.
overview: The Chief trail climbs the back of the granite monolith to three summits above town and Howe Sound. Linking all three peaks makes a short, punchy mountain run. It is also the descent for every climbing route on the Chief.
route_description: From the campground the trail climbs steep wooden stairs through forest, then splits for the First, Second and Third Peaks. Chains and ladders help on the rock sections near the top.
hazards: Slick rock and cliffs near the summits, crowds on weekends, and heat on the exposed granite.
skills: Hiking fitness; care on exposed rock.
go_guided: Pair it with a climb, or join a guided Sea to Sky running day.

name: Sea to Summit Trail
access: Sea to Sky Gondola base, Squamish
summary: A steep climb from sea level to the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola, with a ride back down.

route_description: The trail leaves the gondola base, climbs past Shannon Falls and up steep forested slopes and slabs to the summit lodge. Most people ride the gondola down.

name: Tantalus Range from the Haberl Hut
access: Helicopter from Squamish to the Jim Haberl Hut
summary: Steep glacier skiing from the ACC's Jim Haberl Hut, between Serratus and Dione: Dione's east face, Serratus' north face and Alpha's west couloir.

name: Tantalus Traverse
access: Helicopter from Squamish Airport
summary: The iconic skyline of the Sea to Sky: steep granite and wild glaciers over Tantalus, Dione, Serratus and Alpha.
overview: The traverse links the main summits of the Tantalus Range in two big days, with views from Whistler to Nanaimo and Vancouver and a bivy under the stars. A helicopter in and out keeps the packs light and turns a week-long expedition into a weekend.
route_description: Day one flies to the Serratus/Dione col to stash overnight gear, then climbs the north side of Mount Tantalus and follows the ridge over Dione to camp. Day two continues over Serratus and Alpha before a flight back to Squamish.

name: Garibaldi Neve Traverse
access: Diamond Head trailhead (Squamish) to Rubble Creek, with a car shuttle. Chains are mandatory on the Diamond Head road October to May. The Elfin Lakes shelter and Garibaldi Lake camping must be reserved with BC Parks. The Rubble Creek road isn't plowed in winter, so the trip ends with a road walk.
summary: A big glaciated traverse from Diamond Head to Garibaldi Lake, mostly across the Garibaldi Neve icefield.
overview: The Neve Traverse links the two main entrances to southern Garibaldi Park across one of the corridor's biggest icefields, with Mount Garibaldi on one side and the Sharkfin and Glacier Pikes on the other. Spring brings the best mix of daylight and a stable snowpack.
route_description: The route climbs from the Diamond Head trailhead along Paul Ridge to Elfin Lakes, drops to Ring Creek beneath several avalanche paths, then climbs onto the Garibaldi Neve. The icefield passes Mount Garibaldi and the Sharkfin before crossing a pass west of the Glacier Pikes and descending the Sentinel Glacier to Garibaldi Lake, which needs to be frozen to cross. The final kilometres down to Rubble Creek are often bare trail, followed by a walk out the unplowed access road.
hazards: Avalanche paths above the approach to Ring Creek, crevasses between the Tent and the Sharkfin, whiteouts on the icefield, unfrozen lake ice and a long way from help.
skills: Solid fitness, map and GPS navigation, glacier travel and crevasse rescue, winter camping.
go_guided: A custom trip for a small group, timed for a high-pressure window.
author: Ross Berg

name: Diamond Head & Elfin Lakes
access: Diamond Head trailhead above Squamish, 16 km up the access road; chains are mandatory October to May. The Elfin Lakes shelter must be reserved with BC Parks year-round.
summary: Squamish's local backcountry: a long, gentle climb along Paul Ridge to the Elfin Lakes shelter and the rolling terrain around Round Mountain.
overview: Diamond Head is one of the few places near Squamish where you can reach the alpine on skis or snowshoes without serious avalanche terrain for most of the way. It suits a first overnight, AST field days and non-technical winter summits like Round Mountain. The Elfin Lakes shelter is run by BC Parks and must be reserved.
route_description: The winter route follows the access road to the Red Heather day shelter, then a line of poles along Paul Ridge over Round Mountain to Elfin Lakes. The gentle bowls off Round Mountain suit first turns, while the Gargoyles and Columnar Peak beyond hold longer, steeper runs.

name: Mount Garibaldi
grade: Glaciated snow route, bergschrund, snow and ice to 45°
season: July is best; into September depending on snow
access: 4x4 road up Brohm Ridge (Cheekye FSR Branch 01) north of Squamish, or helicopter. No vehicles past the last gate at about km 11.
summary: The volcano above Squamish: a two-day glacier climb up the Warren Glacier to the north-east face and summit.
overview: Garibaldi is the big white mountain you see from the Squamish Chief. It is a true glacier climb with crevasses and a bergschrund, but technically moderate, which makes it a classic first glaciated summit. July is the best month. It is also skied in spring.
route_description: The approach follows the Brohm Ridge road and ridge over the Shark's Fin to a camp on the moraines beside the Warren Glacier. Summit day climbs the Warren Glacier to the north-east face, crosses the bergschrund and finishes on snow and ice up to 45 degrees, returning the same way.
hazards: Crevasses, the bergschrund, frequent whiteouts, and loose volcanic rock.
skills: Fitness for two big days; glacier skills are taught on the trip. Max 2 guests per guide on summit day.
go_guided: Our two-day trip camps on the mountain; a one-day heli-assisted option is available.
author: Ross Berg

name: Black Tusk
access: Rubble Creek trailhead, Garibaldi Park
summary: A long day to the volcanic spire that marks the Sea to Sky skyline, via Taylor Meadows and Garibaldi Lake.
overview: The Black Tusk is one of the most recognisable summits in BC. The trail climbs through forest and alpine meadows to the base of the tower. The final chimney is a scramble on loose rock that many parties skip.
route_description: From Rubble Creek the trail climbs switchbacks to Taylor Meadows and Garibaldi Lake, then up to the base of the Tusk. Most parties return the same way.
hazards: Loose rock and exposure on the final scramble, heat, and BC Parks day-use pass requirements.
skills: Good fitness for a big day.

name: Panorama Ridge
access: Rubble Creek trailhead, Garibaldi Park
summary: The best view in Garibaldi Park: the turquoise Garibaldi Lake from the top of Panorama Ridge.
overview: Panorama Ridge is a big day out with one of the most photographed views in the province. It shares the approach with Black Tusk and makes a fine long run.
route_description: The trail climbs from Rubble Creek to Taylor Meadows, then continues through Helmet junction and up the ridge to the summit. Return the same way.

skills: Good fitness for a long day.

name: Elfin Lakes
access: Diamond Head trailhead above Squamish
summary: Squamish's easiest way into the alpine on foot: a long, runnable ridge to two small lakes under Garibaldi's south side.
overview: If you want alpine views from Squamish without a scramble or a 4 a.m. start, this is the one. The old access road means the climb is steady and almost all runnable, and Paul Ridge opens up early with Garibaldi and the Gargoyles in front of you. It's a long day for the views it gives, which is why we'd run it rather than hike it.
route_description: The route climbs the Diamond Head road and trail through forest to the Red Heather day shelter, then follows Paul Ridge across open meadows to the Elfin Lakes shelter. Most runners turn around at the lakes. Strong parties carry on toward Opal Cone for a longer day.
hazards: Exposure on Paul Ridge in bad weather, snow lingering into July, and bears in the meadows.
skills: Fitness for a long, steady day; basic navigation if the cloud comes in on the ridge.
go_guided: A good first Coast Mountain run with a guide, and an easy one to pair with a skills session on pacing and fuelling.

name: Garibaldi Lake Circumnavigation
time: Our track: 25 h car to car, non-stop
access: Rubble Creek trailhead (Garibaldi Lake parking), Highway 99
summary: A full loop around Garibaldi Lake from Rubble Creek: 56 km and about 4,500 m of climbing, tracked by our guides in one 25-hour push.
overview: Garibaldi Lake is the classic overnight hike in Garibaldi Park. This loop goes round the whole basin instead, linking the high ground on every side of the lake and topping out at 2,670 m on the east side. It's a big mountain day for strong, self-sufficient parties: long, remote and committing once you leave the trails.

skills: Fast, efficient movement over rough alpine terrain, navigation, and the fitness for a 20-plus-hour day.
go_guided: We can guide it as a custom mountain-running or alpine day for strong parties.

name: Spearhead Traverse
access: Blackcomb lifts out, Whistler lifts home (WB backcountry ticket)
summary: The Sea to Sky's signature ski traverse: a horseshoe of glaciers and cols linking Blackcomb to Whistler around the Fitzsimmons valley.
overview: The Spearhead leaves the top of Blackcomb and circles the head of Fitzsimmons Creek over a dozen-plus glaciers before dropping back to Whistler Mountain. Lifts at both ends mean the whole loop stays high, which is what makes it feel like a European haute route in our own backyard. The Spearhead Huts Society's Kees and Claire Hut above Russet Lake sits near the Whistler end and is booked online.
route_description: The first day crosses the Blackcomb and Decker glaciers into the heart of the range. The middle of the route links a series of glaciers and short climbs to cols under Tremor, Ripsaw and Fitzsimmons. The final leg climbs past Russet Lake and follows the Musical Bumps ridge back to Whistler's lifts.
hazards: Crevasses, avalanche slopes above and below the route, cornices on cols, and whiteouts on broad glaciers where navigation errors are common.
skills: AST 1 minimum, glacier travel and crevasse rescue, whiteout navigation, comfortable skiing variable snow with a pack.
go_guided: We keep dates flexible and go on the best-weather window, and we carry the rescue kit and the navigation load so you can enjoy the skiing.

name: Musical Bumps to Russet Lake
access: Whistler Mountain lifts (WB backcountry ticket)
summary: A rolling alpine ridge from the top of Whistler, past Flute and over Oboe, toward Singing Pass and Russet Lake.
overview: The Musical Bumps is the gentler half of the Whistler backcountry: a ridge walk on skis with laps off each bump and big views of the Spearhead and Black Tusk. It is also the last leg of the Spearhead Traverse and the usual way into the Kees and Claire Hut for an overnight.
route_description: From the top of Symphony Express the ridge runs past Flute, still inside the resort boundary, then leaves the ski area and climbs over Oboe toward Singing Pass. Parties either lap the bowls off the ridge and head back toward the resort, or carry on to Russet Lake for a night at the hut.
hazards: Whiteout navigation on a broad ridge is the classic problem here, plus avalanche slopes off each side of the bumps and a long exit if the weather turns.
skills: AST 1, solid navigation in poor visibility, comfortable touring and skiing off-piste.

name: Blackcomb & Decker Glaciers
access: Blackcomb lifts (WB backcountry ticket)

name: Musical Bumps to Singing Pass

name: Pencil Couloir, Mount Currie

overview: Mount Currie offers some of the biggest ski vertical in the corridor, and the Pencil is its most famous line. It is a committing objective that needs the right snowpack, the right temperatures and a fit, efficient team.
route_description: The Pencil is a long, narrow slot on Currie's north face, entered from high on the mountain above Pemberton. Most parties start with a helicopter lift from Pemberton and a bootpack to the top; parties on foot climb from the valley and often camp high to catch the snow at the right time. Below the couloir, the descent continues down avalanche gullies and forest to logging roads on the valley floor, more than 2000 m below the top.
hazards: A funnelled terrain trap, large avalanche paths overhead, sluff and long exposure to warming slopes.
skills: Expert steep skiing, AST 2 level judgement, crampon and axe use.
go_guided: Guided ascents are timed for a stable spring window with an early start.

name: Keith's Hut & Cerise Creek
grade: Moderate glacier touring; Birthday Chute about 40–45°
time: Full day, or 2–3 days from the hut
access: Cerise Creek trailhead off Highway 99 (Duffey Lake Road), north of Pemberton. The old Cerise Creek FSR is decommissioned and can't be driven; park on the widened highway shoulder.
summary: Cerise Creek is the Duffey's classic hut-based ski touring basin, with Keith's Hut below the Anniversary Glacier giving access to Vantage, Joffre, Matier and the Birthday Chute.
overview: It's a short skin to the hut, then a lot of terrain: the Anniversary Glacier, Vantage Peak and its shoulder, and big lines on Joffre and Matier. The Duffey is drier and colder than Whistler, so the snowpack behaves differently from the coast. The hut is first come, first served and fills on powder weekends, so carry a tent.
route_description: From the highway, a forested approach climbs gently up Cerise Creek to Keith's Hut (Keith Flavelle Memorial Hut, about 1,650 m) at the toe of the Anniversary Glacier. The winter route crosses debris from the 2019 Joffre Peak landslides. Above the hut, the glacier and the Vantage shoulder offer mellow glacier runs and steeper couloirs, including the Birthday Chute, a narrow 40–45° chute that opens into a big fan. Joffre and Matier hold bigger alpine objectives for strong parties in stable conditions.
hazards: Avalanche terrain and runout paths above the approach, cornices, crevasses on the Anniversary Glacier, the closed slide path below Joffre Peak, creek crossings in spring, thin snow at chute entrances early season, and car break-ins at Duffey trailheads.
skills: Solid off-piste skiing, AST 1 minimum (AST 2 for steep objectives), glacier travel and crevasse rescue. Ice axe and crampons for the chutes.
go_guided: We run custom hut and day trips to Cerise Creek and summer mountaineering in the Joffre group.

name: Stairmaster Couloir & Corona Bowl

summary: Stairmaster Couloir is a steep bootpack couloir to the summit of Phalanx Mountain in the Blackcomb backcountry, often linked with a run down Corona Bowl.
overview: This is a big day out of the Blackcomb lifts, not a sidecountry lap. The Stairmaster is a sustained bootpack that earns its name and puts you on top of Phalanx with the glacier below. Corona Bowl has seen several big avalanches over the years, so save it for a stable day and good visibility.
route_description: The day starts from the top of the Blackcomb lifts and crosses the Spearhead Glacier toward Phalanx Mountain (2,441 m) at the north end of the Spearhead Range. The Stairmaster Couloir is a narrow, steep gully through the cliff bands toward Phalanx's double summit. Descents include the Phalanx Glacier and Corona Bowl, which skis back toward Blackcomb's boundary.
hazards: Large avalanche paths (Corona Bowl has had several involvements), a steep confined couloir with no escape, cornices, crevasses on the Spearhead and Phalanx glaciers, flat light, and a long, bushy exit if you miss the line off Phalanx.
skills: Expert off-piste skiing, AST 2 recommended, glacier travel and crevasse rescue, and ice axe and crampon use for the bootpack.

name: Callaghan Valley & Journeyman Lodge

summary: Off-grid lodge touring in the upper Callaghan Valley near Whistler: north-facing trees and alpine terrain, reached by snowcat or a 13 km ski in.
overview: The Callaghan gets more snow than Whistler village and none of the sled traffic from the neighbouring valleys. The ridgeline from Journeyman Peak to the Solitude Glacier gives about 8 km of north-facing tree lines back to the lodge door, which makes it one of the best storm-day setups around. Above them, Journeyman Peak and the Solitude Glacier offer alpine terrain, with Hidden Peak and Callaghan Peak further out.

name: Widow Maker Arete
time: Long day (10+ hours from the Grouse gondola)
access: Grouse Mountain gondola, then trails via Little Goat and Crown Pass into Hanes Valley
summary: Widow Maker Arete is a 5.9 alpine rock route on the northeast arete of Crown Mountain to The Camel, the closest real alpine climb to downtown Vancouver.
overview: A real alpine route you can reach from the Grouse gondola. The climbing is mostly easy slab and ridge with a few steep 5.8–5.9 steps, and the rock is mostly good with some loose blocks. The approach and descent take more of the day than the climbing, so don't let the modest grade fool you.
route_description: From the top of Grouse, trails cross toward Little Goat and drop to Crown Pass, then descend partway into Hanes Valley before climbing scree and talus to the base of Crown Mountain's northeast arete. Long stretches of 3rd and 4th class slab and ridge link short steep sections of finger cracks, blocky face and a wide crack near the top. The route finishes on The Camel beside Crown's summit, and rappels lead to the summit trail back to Grouse.
hazards: Loose blocks, route-finding (there has been a fatal accident off route), old fixed webbing at the rappels, late-season snow at the first headwall, scree on the approach, and steep, muddy trails at Crown Pass. Hanes Valley is a frequent North Shore Rescue callout area.
skills: To follow: comfortable seconding 5.9 and moving unroped on exposed 3rd–4th class. To lead: 5.9 trad, with efficient simul-climbing, rappelling and alpine rope work.
go_guided: We guide it as a custom alpine climbing day.

name: Prow Wall
access: Stawamus Chief, via the Apron and South Gully
summary: The Prow Wall is a steep, hard multi-pitch wall high on the Stawamus Chief. Its easiest line, Unbearable, goes at 5.12a; everything else is 5.13 or harder.
overview: This is the Chief's upper tier for strong climbers. You reach it by climbing an Apron route and hiking into South Gully, so it feels more remote than a wall above town should. Unbearable is the way in for 5.12 climbers; the original Prow Wall line went free at 5.14a.
route_description: The Prow Wall rises left of South Gully, across from the Squamish Buttress and right of the Echelon Wall. Most routes climb steep corner systems on the right side, including Unbearable (5.12a), Teddy Bear's Picnic and Gravity Bong (about 5.13a), and on the left Written in Stone (5.11d). The original Prow Wall route is eight pitches, about 200 m. Climbers walk off across the top toward the Chief's summit trails.
hazards: Loose blocks and fixed lines of unknown condition in South Gully, loose rock on the ledge above the first pitch, seepage after rain, and a committing position high on the Chief.
skills: To follow: top-roped 5.11+ on steep cracks and corners. To lead: 5.12a trad for Unbearable; most other lines need 5.13a and up.
go_guided: Strong climbers can book a custom multi-pitch day to work up to the Prow Wall with a guide.
author: Ross Berg

name: Teddy Bear's Picnic
access: Stawamus Chief, via the Apron and South Gully
summary: Teddy Bear's Picnic is a steep crack-and-corner line on the Chief's Prow Wall. Finished via Unbearable it goes at 5.12a, on some of the best rock in Squamish.
overview: Our guides came back raving about this one. The Elevator Shaft pitch is three-dimensional 5.11c stemming you won't find anywhere else on the Chief. Most parties finish on Unbearable at 5.12a; the original laser crack and changing corners are harder, around 5.12d/5.13a.
route_description: Established by Jeremy Blumel and Adam Diamond, the route starts from the shared access pitch in South Gully. The signature pitch is the Elevator Shaft, a deep slot at about 5.11c. From there the original line follows a laser-cut crack and changing corners, while Evan Stevens' Unbearable finish goes through a slot and roof at 5.12a to the top. You walk off toward the Chief's summit trails.
hazards: Loose rock in South Gully and on the first ledge, fixed lines of unknown condition, a committing position high on the wall, and seepage after rain.
skills: To follow: top-roped 5.12 on steep corners and roofs. To lead: 5.12a trad (Unbearable finish); the original line is about 5.12d/5.13a.
go_guided: Book a custom multi-pitch day if you climb solid 5.11+ and want a guide on the Prow Wall.

name: Great Drain to The Great Game
access: Slhanay, off the Mamquam FSR
summary: Great Drain to The Great Game is a five-pitch Slhanay linkup with a bolted squeeze, steep cracks and Great Game's juggy 5.10c finish, a shady escape from Chief crowds.
overview: Slhanay is the quiet, shady face north of the Chief, so this is a good call on a hot July day when the Apron is cooking. Expect wide flakes and a short bolted squeeze on The Great Drain before the linkup traverses onto The Great Game for the best finish on the wall. It's steeper and easier than it looks from the base.
route_description: The Great Drain starts just right of The Great Game, where the Slhanay trail meets the wall. It climbs a 5.7 corner, a wide flake into a bolt-protected squeeze chimney and hollow flakes, then a short bolted slab traverses left to join The Great Game. The final pitch is steep and juggy past two bolts, then eases onto a long ramp; about 120 m in all. The descent trail on the right side of the formation includes a 4th-class chimney with a fixed line.
hazards: Hollow flakes on the third pitch, the 4th-class chimney on the descent, and an approach road and trail that can be overgrown.
skills: To follow: top-roped 5.10 cracks and comfort in a short squeeze chimney. To lead: 5.10c trad.
go_guided: Book a custom multi-pitch day, or build crack and gear skills first on our trad course.

name: Star Chek
access: Cheakamus Canyon (The Gorge), off Highway 99 north of Squamish
summary: Star Chek is a four-pitch, fully bolted 5.9 that climbs out of the Cheakamus Canyon right above the river, one of the few bolted multi-pitch routes near Squamish.
overview: The obvious first bolted multi-pitch near Squamish. The pitches are short, but the position over the roaring Cheakamus feels much bigger than the grade. It's popular, so go early or midweek, and watch for rockfall from people above you.
route_description: Star Chek climbs Galaxy Buttress in The Gorge, about 28 km north of Squamish. Four short bolted pitches of about 20–25 m go 5.8, 5.7, 5.7, then a 5.9 finish, with a 5.8 bolted alternative (The HOV Lane) and a 5.10c variation (Chek it Out) for the last pitch. The base is reached by a short trail over scree from the highway turnout or by rappelling in, and the route tops out near the highway.
hazards: Loose rock near the top falling on parties below, rappelling in on top of other climbers, an unstable scree approach, high spring water in the Cheakamus, and highway parking.
skills: To follow: top-roped 5.8. To lead: 5.9 sport, with confident rappelling and multi-pitch changeovers.
go_guided: A good first multi-pitch on a custom day, and a great objective after our multi-pitch course.
author: Ross Berg

name: Exasperator
access: Grand Wall base, Stawamus Chief
summary: Exasperator is a 45 m 5.10c finger crack at the base of the Grand Wall, one of Canada's classic trad pitches. Bring lots of small nuts and trust your feet.
overview: It looks short from the ground; it isn't. The first section is a straight crack to a stance, then the crack jogs right for about 6 m of delicate fingerlocks on smears, and that's where most people fall. Expect a queue on a sunny weekend.
route_description: Exasperator is the first distinct crack right of the Peasant's Route dihedral in the Grand Wall base area. It's 45 m, usually split into two pitches, though many climbers link them on a 60 m rope. The upper section jogs right on thin fingers and smears, then back left as the crack widens to thin hands. Descend with two rappels, or one with double ropes.
hazards: Crowds at the base, small gear that needs precise placements, a 60 m rope to link the pitches, and possible rockfall closures in the Grand Wall area.
skills: To follow: top-roped 5.10 finger cracks. To lead: 5.10c trad with confident small nut and cam placement.
go_guided: A great day out on a custom single-pitch day, or practise the gear skills first on our trad course.
author: Ross Berg

name: Showcase Spire
time: Half to full day (about 1.5 h approach from the lifts)
season: Spring to late summer, while the Blackcomb lifts run
access: Blackcomb Gondola and Seventh Heaven chair, then across to the Horstman Glacier and the top of the Showcase lift
summary: An 80 m granite spire behind Blackcomb's Showcase lift: rappel into the notch, climb two short pitches of 5.9, then ride a Tyrolean back across.
overview: Showcase Spire is the best short adventure on Blackcomb. It stands apart from the ridge between the Horstman and Blackcomb glaciers, so the only way off the top is a Tyrolean back across the gap, and that ride is why people go. Even on a busy summer day on the mountain you can have it to yourselves.
route_description: From the top of the Blackcomb lifts the approach crosses to the Horstman Glacier and the top of the Showcase lift, then follows the ridge north to the spire. A rope is fixed to bolts on the ridge and the party rappels into the notch below the tower. Two short pitches of 5.9 lead to a small summit with a fixed anchor, where the fixed rope becomes a Tyrolean back to the ridge. The steeper south face has bolted routes around 5.11.
hazards: Rigging mistakes on the Tyrolean, high loads on the anchors, rope sag on the ridge side, exposure in the notch, and lift closing times.
skills: To follow: top-roped 5.9 and comfort with exposure. To lead: 5.9 trad and confident rope rigging for a retrievable Tyrolean.
go_guided: A guide rigs the Tyrolean and keeps the day inside lift hours, so you get the fun without the rope puzzles.
author: Ross Berg

name: Mount Tricouni South Ridge
access: 4x4 road west of Highway 99, between Squamish and Whistler; about 30 minutes on foot to Tricouni Lake
summary: The easier way up Tricouni: a scramble up the south ridge above Tricouni Lake to a summit over the Squamish and Whistler valleys.
overview: The South Ridge is Tricouni's gentler side and the usual way down after the North Ridge. A short walk from the 4x4 road, a small glacier and scrambling on the upper ridge make it a good first alpine day. Our October 2013 trip found 50–80 cm of new snow hiding the crevasses, a reminder that the season ends early up here.
route_description: From the end of the 4x4 road a short trail reaches Tricouni Lake. The route climbs above the lake onto the south ridge, which some parties link with the east ridge, and follows it on 3rd and 4th class ground to the summit. Descent is usually the same way.
hazards: Loose rock and exposure on the ridge, a small glacier with crevasses hidden after new snow, early-season snow, and the 4x4 road.
skills: Comfortable scrambling on exposed rock and basic glacier travel; fitness for a full day.
go_guided: A guide picks the line on the day and ropes up where it matters. Pair it with the North Ridge for a bigger day.
